title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
carry: welcome it, then let it go
tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, and the baby girl who rose from Kamsa's hands. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Did good come from an unexpected direction? Day six hundred eighty-five.

The tenth day. The streets that welcomed Ganesha with drums are full again, louder than before. Trucks carry giant pandal images inch by inch toward the sea. Families carry small ones in their arms. Kids ride on shoulders. And over everything, one call, shouted by huge crowds at once, in Marathi: Ganpati Bappa Morya! And the crowd answers with the second half, which is the part that surprises people. It isn't goodbye. It's come back soon.
screen: `THE TENTH DAY.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA!` → `NOT GOODBYE. COME BACK SOON.`

segments.voice: The full call goes: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Ganpati, our dear father, Morya: next year, come early. Bappa is an affectionate Marathi word, like dad. Morya is often linked to Morya Gosavi, a devoted Ganesha saint remembered at Chinchwad near Pune, whose name became part of the cry. So in one breath, the crowd calls Ganesha family, remembers a devotee, and asks him to hurry back. The last day of the big festival is Anant Chaturdashi, the fourteenth. Before the image leaves home, the family gathers for a final aarti, offers him food for the road, often curd rice or modaks, and asks forgiveness for anything they did wrong as hosts. Then out the door. At the water's edge, the image is turned to face the house or the crowd one last time, then carried in, and slowly let go. People cry at this. Grown men cry at this. Ten days ago he was clay from a shop; now losing him feels like seeing off a relative at the station. That's the heart of what the festival teaches. Love for something doesn't depend on keeping it. The whole ritual is built around loving the guest fully, then letting him go fully, then looking forward. The word visarjan is often translated immersion, but its root sense is closer to letting go, releasing. And the crowd's answer to letting go isn't despair. It's: come back soon. We'll be here.
screen: `BAPPA: DEAR FATHER.` · `MORYA: A SAINT'S NAME IN THE CRY.` · `FOOD FOR THE ROAD, AND FORGIVENESS.` · `LOVE DOESN'T DEPEND ON KEEPING.` · then, large: `COME BACK SOON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who left recently: a visit that ended, a friend who moved, a child back at school. Picture the moment at the door. This time, before they go, thank them silently for coming. Then, on an out-breath, say inwardly what the crowd says: come back soon. Let the breath carry the looking forward. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. It ends with visarjan, a final aarti, food for the road, and the cry Ganpati Bappa Morya: come back soon.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Today, when something good ends, a visit, a call, a day off, say see you soon instead of goodbye. Day six hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: On the last day of Ganesh Chaturthi, often Anant Chaturdashi, families perform a final aarti, offer food for the journey, ask forgiveness for any lapse as hosts, and carry the image to water, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya.

fork.setup: it's the last day. your family's Ganesha is about to leave home for the water. what do many families do first?
options: a final aarti, food for the road, and asking forgiveness.
leave him at home one more year.
fork.reveal: they send him off like a dear guest: fed, thanked, and asked to forgive their lapses.

original.note: Marathi: Ganpati, dear father, Morya. the cry continues: pudhchya varshi lavkar ya, come early next year.

trapdoor: what you thought: the immersion is the sad end of the festival.
what it means: it's a loving farewell that already asks him back next year.
what a scholar hears: Morya in the cry is commonly traced to Morya Gosavi of Chinchwad, a Ganapatya saint; Anant Chaturdashi marks the end of the ten-day public festival.
